content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposed a strong baseline defense, the K-nearest neighbor (KNN) based data filtering against clean-label poisoning attack, which aims to add small noises to (a subset of) training data but maintain the original training labels such that some targeted images at inference will be misclassified. The authors provide geometric interpretations of why K-NN is a good defense and also compare the defense performance against several baselines, including L2 Defense, Robust Feature Extractor, One-Class SVM, and Random Defense. The proposed defense outperforms the compared defense methods by a large factor.

In general, this paper is well-motivated. The defense is simple yet quite effective. However, based on the current presentation, I have the following concerns.

1. The scope of this paper can be limited since it only focuses on defending against one type of attack (clean-label poisoning attack) in the family of data poisoning attacks. It will be great if the authors can further motivate how the KNN defense can be used in a broader context.

2. It is good to see simple methods like KNN turns out to be a strong defense in this context. However, I am wondering how easy it is to bypass this defense. For example, when crafting clean-label poisoning attack, it should be possible to consider a more insidious setting that the added perturbations will make the K-nearest neighbors of the perturbed training samples belong to the target class label (similar to how targeted adversarial examples work). In this case, this defense may be in vain. There are some prior works that study how robust KNN algorithms are when used as a defense, such as "On the Robustness of Deep K-Nearest Neighbors" by Sitawarin and Wagner. Since the proposed defense is "simple" enough so that the attacker may use it as a baseline defense to propose stronger attacks, I believe it's necessary to verify how "easy" it is to be bypassed. Otherwise, technical insights can be limited.

3. How does the proposed defense compare to the data filtering approach used in"Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks" by Tran et al?  Can it be also used as a baseline defense?

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments. Due to the time involved with incorporating their suggested revisions, we have decided to withdraw our paper for this cycle. That said, our responses to the reviewer's comments are posted below.

1. The scope of this paper can be limited since it only focuses on defending against one type of attack (clean-label poisoning attack) in the family of data poisoning attacks. It will be great if the authors can further motivate how the KNN defense can be used in a broader context.

While the kNN defense is useful for detecting poison instances in our paper, more generally it is useful for detecting anomalous instances in the training data which might be incorrectly labeled or of poor quality. We will include a discussion of this in the paper

2. It is good to see simple methods like KNN turns out to be a strong defense in this context. However, I am wondering how easy it is to bypass this defense. For example, when crafting clean-label poisoning attack, it should be possible to consider a more insidious setting that the added perturbations will make the K-nearest neighbors of the perturbed training samples belong to the target class label (similar to how targeted adversarial examples work). In this case, this defense may be in vain.

It is unclear to us the type of attack the reviewer is suggesting here. Placing examples into the training set does not affect **ground truth** label of other training points in its neighborhood. It can, however, manipulate the predicted class of **test** points in its neighborhood, which is exactly how the clean-label attack works.

Targeted adversarial examples manipulate the current test input to cause it to be misclassified as a class of the attacker’s choice. It is unclear to us how this can be extended to clean-label data poisoning since we do not allow the test input to be manipulated.

There are some prior works that study how robust KNN algorithms are when used as a defense, such as "On the Robustness of Deep K-Nearest Neighbors" by Sitawarin and Wagner. Since the proposed defense is "simple" enough so that the attacker may use it as a baseline defense to propose stronger attacks, I believe it's necessary to verify how "easy" it is to be bypassed. Otherwise, technical insights can be limited.

This is a good suggestion and we will add it to future work in this area.

3. How does the proposed defense compare to the data filtering approach used in"Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks" by Tran et al?  Can it be also used as a baseline defense?

This is a good suggestion and we will add it to future work in this area.

content.review:
In this paper, the authors propose a simple and effective method to address the problem of targeted clean-label poisoning where the adversary injects a few samples into the training data thus causing the deployed model to misclassify a particular test sample during inference. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed defenses are able to detect over 99% of poisoning examples. The paper is clearly written by addressing an important problem but I still have several concerns:
1.	In general, the Knn is sensitive to the parameter k, which is not robust in some cases. The authors are expected to clarify how to set the proper parameters especially for the complex tasks. 
2.	The authors are expected to make more comprehensive evaluations to demonstrate their advantages compared with alternative methods, and the effectiveness to other poisoning attacks. 
3.	It is supposed that the performance highly relies on the feature extraction and the authors are expected to further justify how the performance would be if the features are not reliable due to the adversarial attacks.

content.title: Thank you for the helpful review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments. Due to the time involved with incorporating their suggested revisions, we have decided to withdraw our paper for this cycle. That said, our responses to the reviewer's comments are posted below.

1.	In general, the Knn is sensitive to the parameter k, which is not robust in some cases. The authors are expected to clarify how to set the proper parameters especially for the complex tasks.

Actually the defense is quite robust to the choice of k. Beyond k > 500 and up to k = 10000, the attack success rate is near zero while the validation accuracy varies by less than 1%, showing little dependence on k in this large range.

The reason for this is as follows (and also described in Section 4.2). Assume that the data is well clustered such that the average intraclass distance is much larger than the average interclass distance (in feature space. We find this to be empirically true for well-trained networks. If n poisons lie in the midst of the target class examples (by nature of the feature collision attack), then those n poisons are guaranteed to be detected as long as k >= 2*n, since there can be a maximum of n-1 poisons in the neighborhood of a single poison, and thus majority label in that neighborhood will still be the target class. The upper limit is k < 2*c where c is the number of training examples in the current class. Within this limit, a clean target instance’s neighborhood majority label will still be the target class, so the clean target instance is not removed.

We will make this point clearer in the paper so that the reader knows our defense is not very sensitive to the hyperparameter choice.
 
2.	The authors are expected to make more comprehensive evaluations to demonstrate their advantages compared with alternative methods, and the effectiveness to other poisoning attacks. 

We have already compared our defenses to several other baselines (L2, SVM, random point eviction, and no defense), and each of these defenses were run on two of the most popular clean-label attacks from the literature (Shafahi et al. 2018 and Zhu et al. 2019). Both the defense effectiveness and validation performance of the resultant model were evaluated against all these conditions. See Tables 1 and 2 and Section 5.1 and 5.2.

3.	It is supposed that the performance highly relies on the feature extraction and the authors are expected to further justify how the performance would be if the features are not reliable due to the adversarial attacks. 

Our defense is a defense against clean-label attacks, all of which currently rely on perturbing the poisoning instance to have a feature representation close to that of the target instance. This is a common property without which the attacks in their current form would not work. Our defense exploits this common property of the poison instances for detecting them.

We will add a Threat Model section into our paper to clarify our assumptions about the attacker, particularly that they are employing a clean-label attack which relies on feature space similarity between poisons and target.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2

content.review:
This paper demonstrated that the simple k-NN baseline approach provides an effective defense against clean-label poisoning attacks with minimal degradation in model performance. The k-NN defense mechanism identifies virtually all poisons from two state-of-the-art clean label data poisoning attacks, while only filtering a small percentage of non-poisons. The k-NN defense outperforms other simple baselines against the existing attacks

1.  I am not at all familiar with clean-label attack methods, therefore no knowledge of relevant related works. 
These papers seem to follow a pattern that : one propose an attack, and another paper proposes a defense. They do point out the potential issues on non-natural samples, however, only having results from CIFAR-10 certainly weakened the significance or the contribution of this paper. 

2. It does not provide good intuitions or theoretical reasons why such attacks exist and why a simple kNN based method can defend against those attacks. 

3. I hope the authors can provide a more thorough survey of related works. 

4. The experiments seems quite messy, with unfinished analysis and ill-positioned figures. 

5. The proposed defense showed only empirical results against the target attack. It seems to provide no theoretical / provable guarantees.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments. Due to the time involved with incorporating their suggested revisions, we have decided to withdraw our paper for this cycle. That said, our responses to the reviewer's comments are posted below.

1.  I am not at all familiar with clean-label attack methods, therefore no knowledge of relevant related works. 
These papers seem to follow a pattern that : one propose an attack, and another paper proposes a defense. They do point out the potential issues on non-natural samples,

If by non-natural samples the reviewer is referring to the target instance, then recall from our introduction that the motivation for data poisoning (as opposed to the much simpler evasion attacks) is that the **test time** instance needs NOT be perturbed in order for it to be misclassified, whereas in evasion it does. Therefore, considering non-natural target instances is unnecessary.

however, only having results from CIFAR-10 certainly weakened the significance or the contribution of this paper. 

We execute our defense on CIFAR-10 since it is the dataset on which prior attacks (Shafahi et al. 2018 and Zhu et al. 2018) were benchmarked.

2. It does not provide good intuitions or theoretical reasons why such attacks exist and why a simple kNN based method can defend against those attacks. 

We hope that our paper can provide intuition and understanding about our results to the reader and we will add a more intuitive explanation of the defenses into the paper.

3. I hope the authors can provide a more thorough survey of related works. 

We will add additional discussion of related works in our current related works section.

4. The experiments seems quite messy, with unfinished analysis and ill-positioned figures. 

We will improve the layout of our paper as well as stylistic issues in our figures.

5. The proposed defense showed only empirical results against the target attack. It seems to provide no theoretical / provable guarantees. 

Certified defenses against evasion adversarial attacks with provable guarantees were introduced only several years after empirical defenses were demonstrated on them. Likewise for poisoning, our work is only the first empirical defense against this important class of poisoning attacks (clean-label) and we hope that follow-on work will include more certified defenses as well.
